definition: Weak, or feeble;
sourceDefinition: Weak, or feeble; (JK, S, Msb, K;) applied to a man; (S;) as also ↓ xaAy^irN , (K,) and ↓ xaw^uwrN : (AHeyth:) a weak man, who cannot endure difficulty or distress: (Lth:) and (tropical:) cowardly, or a coward: (A:) pl. of the first xaw~aAruwna , and of the third xuwarapN . (AHeyth.) Applied to a camel, Slender ( raqiyq ) and beautiful: (K, TA: [for AlHis~i in the CK, I read AlHasanu , as in other copies of the K and in the TA:]) and the fem., with p , applied to a she-camel, having soft flesh and fragile bones: (TA:) pl. of the former [and of the latter] xaw~aAraAtN . (K.) Applied to a spear, Weak: (S:) not hard: (Msb:) or weak and soft; (TA;) and in the same sense applied to an arrow, (A, TA,) as also ↓ xaw^uwrN ; (TA;) and so the fem. of the former, with p , applied to a reed or cane ( qaSabapN ); (A, TA;) and to land or ground ( A^aroDN ) as meaning weak, (S,) or soft: (A, Msb:) pl. ↓ xuwrN . (S.) And xaw~aAru AlEinaAni (tropical:) A horse (A) that turns easily, (JK, A, K,) and runs much: (K:) pl. ↓ xuwrN . (JK, TA.) And bakorapN xaw~aArapN (assumed tropical:) A sheave of a pulley of which the pin runs [or turns ] easily in the checks. (TA.) And AlHa$aAyaA ↓ xuwru Beds, or the like, stuffed with soft substances. (TA, from a trad.) And xaw~aAru AlS~afaA Smooth stones that sound [ when struck ] by reason of their hardness. (IAar.) And zanodN xaw~aArN A znd [q. v.] that emits much fire; syn. qad~aAHN . (AHeyth, K.) [Hence,] huwa xaw~aAru AlEuwdi [meaning (assumed tropical:) He is lavish when asked ]: an expression of dispraise. (TA in art. ksr .) [Hence also,] xaw~aArapN (tropical:) A she-camel abounding with milk; pl. ↓ xuwrN ; (S, K, TA;) which is contr. to rule, and said by MF to be without a parallel: (TA:) and so a ewe or she-goat: (TA:) or a she-camel whose milk flows easily; and so a ewe or she-goat: (A:) or a she-camel thin-skinned, and abounding with milk: (AHeyth:) or one that is of a hue between dustcolour and red, with a thin skin; and such is the most abundant in milk: (Kf:) or of a red colour inclining to dust-colour, thin-skinned, and having long fur with [ coarse ] hair protruding through it, longer than the rest: such a she-camel is less hardy than others, but abounds with milk. (ISk.) Also (tropical:) A palm-tree ( naxolapN ) that bears much fruit. (JK, A, K.) ― -b2- ↓ xuwrN as meaning (assumed tropical:) Women much suspected, on account of their corruptness, (K, TA,) and the weakness of their forbearance, (TA,) is [a pl.] without a sing. (K.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. duruwsN , It (a trace, or mark, or what is termed rasomN , S, A, K, and a house, A, or a thing, M) became effaced, erased, rased, or obliterated; (S, M, A, K;) as also ↓ Andrs , (K, TA,) said of what is termed rsm : (TA:) or it (the trace, or mark, of a house; or what remained, cleaving to the ground, marking the place of a house;) became covered with sand and dust blown over it by the wind: (TA in art. dvr :) or it (an abode, or a place of sojourning,) became effaced, erased, rased, or obliterated, and its traces, or remains, became concealed, or unseen: (Msb:) and darusa signifies the same as darasa in the first of the senses explained above, but in an intensive manner. (M.) ― -b2- [Hence AlA=yaAtu ↓ daArasati as explained near the end of this paragraph.] ― -b3- Hence, also, (AHeyth,) darasa Alv~awobi , (AHeyth, S, A, K,) inf. n. darosN , (S, TA,) (tropical:) The garment, or piece of cloth, became old and worn out. (AHeyth, S, A, K.) ― -b4- And darasa AlkitaAbu (assumed tropical:) The writing, or book, became old. (Msb.) ― -b5- [Hence, also,] darasato , (S, M, A, K,) aor. , (M,) inf. n. duruwsN (S, M, K) and darosN , (M, K,) (tropical:) She (a woman, S, M, A, K, or, accord. to Lh, a girl, M) menstruated. (S, M, A, K.) -A2- darasatohu Alr~iyHu , (S, M, K,) or Alr~iyaAHu , (A,) [aor. ,] inf. n. darosN , (A, TA,) The wind, (S, M, K,) or winds, (A,) effaced, erased, rased, or obliterated, it, (S, M, A, K,) by repeatedly passing over it; (A;) namely, a trace, or mark, [of a house &c.,] or what is termed rasomN ; (S, K;) and [ erased, or rased, ] a house; (A;) or a thing: (M:) and darasahu Alqawomu The people effaced, erased, rased, or obliterated, it. (M.) ― -b2- Hence, (AHeyth,) darasa Alv~awoba , (AHeyth, K,) aor. , inf. n. darosN , (TA,) (tropical:) He rendered the garment, or piece of cloth, old and worn-out. (AHeyth, K.) ― -b3- darasa AlT~aEaAma , (M,) or AlHinoTapa , (S, A, Msb, K,) wanaHowahaA , (Msb,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. darosN (M, K) and diraAsN , (S, A, Msb, K,) (tropical:) He trod, or thrashed, the wheat, (S, M, A, Msb, K,) and the like: (Msb:) [because he who does so passes repeatedly over it:] of the dial. of El-Yemen: (M, TA:) or diraAsN in the sense here indicated is of the dial. of Syria. (TA.) ― -b4- darasa AlmaroA^apa , (A,) or AljaAriyapa , (K,) (tropical:) He compressed the woman, (A,) or the girl. (K.) ― -b5- darasa Aln~aAqapa , (M, A,) aor. , inf. n. darosN , (M,) (tropical:) He broke, or trained, the she-camel: (M, A:) [and so, app., ↓ daArasahaA ; for it is said that] the primary signification of mudaArasapN is the breaking, or training, or disciplining, [a beast;] and returning time after time ( taEah~udN ) to a thing. (TA.) You say also, baEiyrN lamo yudorasu , meaning (tropical:) A camel that has not been ridden. (S, TA.) ― -b6- Hence, (M,) [or from darasatohu Alr~iyHu , or from darasa Alv~awoba ,] darasa AlkitaAba , (S, M, A, K,) aor. (M, K) and , (K,) inf. n. darosN and diraAsapN (S, M, K) and daraAsapN and diraAsN , (TA,) (tropical:) He read the book; (M, K;) as though he opposed it until it became easy for him to remember it: (M:) or he read it repeatedly, [or studied it, ] in order to remember it: (A:) or he made it easy to remember, by much reading: (TA:) or he read and learned it: (Bd in vi. 105:) and ↓ daArasahu , inf. n. mudaArasapN and diraAsN , signifies the same: (M:) and so ↓ daras~ahu , and ↓ A^adorasahu : (K:) or the former of the last two has an intensive signification: the latter of them is mentioned by IJ: (TA:) [but accord. to the M, it is said by IJ that both of these are doubly trans., and have a different signification, which is also indicated in the A as that of the former of them: see 2:] Alkutuba ↓ daArasato , and ↓ tadaArasotuhaA , and ↓ Aid~aArasotuhaA , signify the same as darasotuhaA [ I read the books, or read them repeatedly, &c.]: (S, TA:) and AlquroA=na ↓ tadaArasa signifies He read the Kur-án, and returned to it time after time, in order that he might not forget it. (TA.) You say also, darasotu AlEiloma , aor. , inf. n. darosN and diraAsapN , (tropical:) I read science. (Msb.) It is said in the Kur [vi. 105], accord. to different reading, waliyaquwluwA darasota , and ↓ daArasota , (tropical:) [ And to the end that they may say, Thou hast read, &c.:] but some say that the former means Thou hast read the books of the people of the Scriptures: and the latter, Thou hast consulted, or conferred, with them; expl. by *aAkarotuhumo : (M:) or the former means Thou hast learned: (Abu-l-'Abbás:) and the latter, Thou hast read, or studied, under the Jews as thy teachers, and they have read, or studied, under thee as their teacher: (I'Ab, Mujáhid, K:) and another reading is ↓ daArasa ; i. e. daArasa Aln~abiY~u Alyahuwda [ he prophet hath read, or studied, with the Jews ] : and another, ↓ daArasato , which may be rendered in two ways: The Jews have read, or studied, or consulted, or conferred, with ( daArasato ) Mohammad: and The signs ( A=yaAt ) have vied in length of time [or antiquity ] with those of other scriptures so that every one of them has for the most part become obliterated: (TA:) and another reading is darasato ; and another, darusato ; both meaning, They (these stories, or histories,) have become obliterated: (M:) or they are things which have long since passed: (Abu-l-' Abbás:) but the latter of these two verbs has a more intensive signification: and it is also said to signify They have been dissipated. (M.) [You also say, darasa Ealayohi (tropical:) He read, or studied, under him as his teacher; like qaraA^a Ealayohi .]

sourceDefinition: signifies AlmawotaY ↓ mudaAfanapu [i. e. The cooperating in the burying of the dead ]. (TA.) laA yakaAdu Aln~aAsu yatadaAfanuwna [ The people can hardly, or cannot nearly, bury one another ] is said in the case of a quick and spreading death. (TA voce *ariygN .) ― -b2- [Hence,] tadaAfanuwA (tropical:) They practised concealment, one with another; syn. takaAtamuwA . (S, K, TA.) It is said in a trad., lawo takaA$afotumo lamaA tadaAfanotumo (tropical:) [ If ye revealed, one to another his faults, or his secrets, ye would not practise concealment, one with another, in any case]; meaning, if the fault, ( Eayob , as in my copies of the S and in the TA in the present art.,) or secret or secrets, ( gayob , as in one of my copies of the S in art. k$f ,) of each one of you were open, or revealed, to each other of you: (S, TA:) or, accord. to IAth, [ if ye revealed, one to another his secrets, ye would not bury one another; for he says that] the meaning is, if each one of you knew what is concealed in the mind of each other of you, the conducting of his funeral, and his burial, would be deemed onerous. (TA in art. k$f .)

definition: [ An entrance-passage of a house;
sourceDefinition: [ An entrance-passage of a house; an entrance-hall; a vestibule; ] what is between the [ outer ] door or gate and the house; (S, K;) the place of entrance to a house: (Msb:) a Persian word, (S, Msb,) originally dAlyj , and dAlyz , and dAlAn , and, as some say, daliyjN , (Lth,) arabicized: (Lth, S, Msb:) [also, in modern Arabic, an ante- chamber: and the anterior apartment of a large tent or pavilion: accord. to the MA, a large tent: accord. to some copies of the K, i. q. jayoy^apN : accord. to some, xaniy~apN , which reading is preferred by the author of the TK, who explains dhlyz , from the “Burhán,” as meaning “absurd words:” accord. to some, Haniy~apN , which I think the right reading, meaning a bowed, or curved, structure: Golius seems to have found another reading in the K, namely, Hay~apN :] pl. dahaAliyzu . (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] A^abonaA='u Ald~ahaAliyzi (assumed tropical:) Foundlings, (K, * TA,) whose fathers are unknown. (TA.) [They are so called because they are generally abandoned at the entrances of mosques or private houses, whence they are usually taken by persons who adopt them.]

definition: and ↓ A_idohaAnN signify the same;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ A_idohaAnN signify the same; (S, Msb, K;) i. e. (tropical:) The endeavouring to conciliate; syn. muSaAnaEapN : (S, TA:) or the making peace with another; or becoming reconciled with another: (Msb:) or the pretending the contrary of, or what is different from, that which one conceals in his mind: (K:) and the former signifies also the acting with dishonesty, or dissimulation: or ↓ the latter has this signification; and the former signifies the striving to outwit, deceive, beguile, or circumvent; syn. muwaArabapN : (TA:) or daAhanotu signifies I hid, concealed, or covered; syn. waArayotu [accord. to four copies of the S; but probably this is a mistranscription for waArabotu , meaning I strove to outwit, deceive, beguile, or circumvent, as is indicated in the TA]; and ↓ A^adohanotu signifies I acted with dishonesty, or dissimulation: (S:) or ↓ A_idohaAnN is [originally] like tadohiynN [as has been stated above]: but is used as denoting the act of treating with gentleness or blandishment, soothing, coaxing, wheedling, beguiling, or deluding; and abstaining from restraint or prohibition: (AHeyth, TA:) or it originally signified the anointing such a thing as a hide with some oil or the like : and as such a thing is rendered soft to the sense [of feeling], it was used tropically, or metaphorically, to denote ideal softness, absolutely: hence, the treating with gentleness or blandishment, soothing, coaxing, wheedling, beguiling, or deluding, was termed mudaAhanapN : then this tropical signification became commonly known, and conventionally regarded as proper: and then the word [ mdAhnp or ↓ AdhAn , or rather each of these words,] was tropically used as signifying the holding a thing in light, or little, or mean, estimation, or in contempt: so in the 'Ináyeh. (MF, TA.) It is said in the Kur [lxviii. 9], ↓ wad~uwAlawo tudohinu fayudohinuwna (tropical:) They wish that thou wouldst endeavour to conciliate [them], and in that case they will endeavour to conciliate [thee]: (S, TA: *) or that thou wouldst be soft, pliant, or gentle, in thy religion, and in that case they will be soft, pliant, or gentle: (TA:) or that thou wouldst be soft, pliant, or gentle, to them, and in that case they will be so to thee: (Jel:) or, accord. to Fr, that thou wouldst be an unbeliever, and they will be unbelievers. (TA.)

definition: Whatever one is obliged, or bound, to preserve and guard and defend or protect, (T, M, K, *) and for the loss or neglect of which one must be blamed: (T:) things that are sacred, or inviolable;
sourceDefinition: Whatever one is obliged, or bound, to preserve and guard and defend or protect, (T, M, K, *) and for the loss or neglect of which one must be blamed: (T:) things that are sacred, or inviolable; a man's family, and property ( Hawozap ), and servants or dependents, and relations: (AA, T:) as also ↓ *amaArN : (TA:) things for which, if he did not defend or protect them, a man would be blamed, and severely reproved: (A:) or what is behind a man, [ as a burden upon him, ] of those things which it is his duty to defend or protect; for they say HaAmiYAl*~imaAri , [see below,] like as they say HaAmiY AlHaqiyqapi ; and those things are termed *mAr because anger ( ta*am~urN ) on their account is incumbent on him to whom they pertain; and they are termed Hqyqp because it is the duty of him to whom they pertain to defend them. (S.) HaAmiYAl*~imaAri signifies The defender, or protector, of those things for which a man is to be blamed, and severely reproved, if he do not defend or protect them: (A:) [or of those things which he is bound to preserve and guard and defend, &c.: see above:] or one who, when he is incited, or instigated, and angry, defends, or protects. (S.) One says also, fulaAnN A^amonaEu *imaArFA mino fulaAnK [app., Such a one is a greater defender of those things which it is his duty to defend than such a one ]. (S.) ― -b2- yawomu Al*~imaAri The day of war: or of perdition: or of anger. (Et-Towsheeh.)

definition: A man who inserts his hand into the vulva of a she-camel, to discover if her fœtus be a male or a female: (S, M, K:) because he feels its mu*am~ar , and thus knows it: he feels its jaw-bones: if they be thick, it is a male;
sourceDefinition: A man who inserts his hand into the vulva of a she-camel, to discover if her fœtus be a male or a female: (S, M, K:) because he feels its mu*am~ar , and thus knows it: he feels its jaw-bones: if they be thick, it is a male; and if thin, a female. (M.) El-Kumeyt says, waqaAla Almu*am~iru liln~aAtijiyna mataY *um~irato qaboliYa AlA^arojulu [ And he whose business it was to feel the fœtus, for the purpose of discovering if it were male or female, said to those assisting the she-camels in bringing forth, When, before my time, were the legs felt to discover the sex of the fœtus? ]: (S, M:) for it is the head that is felt, as above explained. (M.) The mu*am~ir is, to camels, as the midwife to human beings. (A.)

A, K,) the former of which is said to be the more chaste, (TA,) The wisp of wool, (T, S, M, A, K,) or piece of rag, (Ks, T, M,) with which one smears with tar a camel (Ks, T, S, M, A, K) that is scabby or mangy: (Ks, T:) of the dial. of Temeem: (M:) also called wafiyEapN [and vamalapN ]. (T.) One says, kaA^an~a EiroDahu ribo*apu AlhaAniY'i [ As though his honour, or reputation, were the rb*p of him who smears camels with tar ]; and in like manner, ribo*apu AlHaAy^iDi [explained below]. (A.) And lam~aA A^asomaEahumu AlHaq~a naba*uwhu kamaA yanobi*u AlhaAniY'u Alr~ibo*apa [ When he made them to hear, or told them, the truth, they rejected it, like as he who smears camels with tar rejects the rb*p after using it]. (A.) ― -b2- Also The piece of rag with which the goldsmith polishes ornaments. (S, L, K, and Msb in explanation of the latter word.) ― -b3- And the former word, The rag of a menstruating woman; (M, A, L, K;) the thing that the menstruating woman throws away. (M, L.) ― -b8- The pl. of ribo*apN in all the senses expl. above is rib*N and ribaA*N (M, L, K.)

(Zj, Msb.) raHaA Alyadi [or raHaY Alyadi ] signifies The hand-mill. (MA.) ― -b2- [Hence, A molar tooth, or grinder: ] i. q. DirosN ; (S, Msb, K;) pl. A^aroHaA='N i. q. (Zj, in his “ Khalk el-Insán. ”) ― -b3- [And app. A roller with which land is rolled to crush the clods; as being likened to a mill-stone: see 1 in art. xtm , near the end of the paragraph.] ― -b4- Stones: and a great rock, or mass of stone. (TA.) ― -b5- A round piece of ground, rising above what surrounds it, (S, K,) about as large in extent as a mile: (K:) pl. A^aroHaA='N : (K, TA:) or this latter, i. e. the pl., signifies pieces of rugged ground, less than mountains, round, and rising above what surrounds them: (M, TA:) or raHFA mina AlA^aroDi means a round and rugged place [or piece of ground ] among sands: (Sh, TA:) or a large and rugged [ elevation such as is termed ] qaArap or A^akamap , round, rising above what surrounds it, not spreading upon the surface of the earth, nor producing herbs, or leguminous plants, nor trees. (ISh, TA.) ― -b6- A round cloud; [as being likened to a mill-stone;] (A in art. rjH :) or so raHaY saHaAbK . (S.) ― -b7- The kirokirap [or callous protuberance upon the breast ] of a camel; (T, S, K;) so called because of its roundness: (TA:) pl. A^aroHaA='N : (K:) which likewise signifies the callous protuberances upon the knees of the camel. (T, TA.) ― -b8- The foot ( firosin ) of the camel and of the elephant: pl. A^aroHaA='N . (M, K.) ― -b9- A daAy^irap [app. meaning a circling border ] around the nail. (TA.) ― -b10- The breast, or chest: pl., as in the other senses following, A^aroHaA='N . (K.) ― -b11- Spinage, or spinach; (M, K;) because of the roundness of its leaves. (TA.) ― -b12- (tropical:) A collective body of the members of a household. (ISd, K, TA.) ― -b13- (tropical:) An independent tribe: (K, TA:) A^aroHaA='N (which is its pl., K, TA) signifies (tropical:) independent tribes, that are in no need of others. (S, TA.) ― -b14- (assumed tropical:) A large number of camels, crowding, or pressing, together; (S, K, TA;) also called TaH~aAnapN : (S, TA:) or raHaA AlA_ibili means the collective herd of the camels: and in like manner, raHaA Alqawomi the collective body of the people, or party. (ISk, TA.) ― -b15- raHaY Alqawomi signifies [also] (tropical:) The chief of the people, or party. (T, S, M, K, TA.) [It is added in the TA that 'Omar Ibn-El-Khattáb was called raHaY AlHarobi , as though meaning (assumed tropical:) The chief of war; because of his warlike propensities: but it seems from what here follows, as well as from what precedes, that this may be a mistranscription, for raHaY Alqawomi or raHaY AlEarabi .] ― -b16- raHaY AlHarobi signifies (tropical:) The most vehement part [or the thickest ] of the fight; syn. (TA.) In a saying relating to 'Alee's having made an end of Aljamali ↓ maroHay , this expression is expl. by A 'Obeyd as meaning The place around which revolved the thickest of the fight ( AlmawoDiEu Al~a*iy daArato Ealayohi raHay AlHarobi ) [in the Battle of the Camel ]. (TA.) And daArato Ealayohi raHay Almawoti [which may be rendered (assumed tropical:) The main stress of death beset him round about ] means death befell him. (Msb, TA.)

(of pauc., S) of raHFY (Msb) [and of raHFA ] is A^aroHK and (of mult., S) A^aroHaA='N , (S, Msb, K,) which latter is the pl. that is preferred accord. to IAmb, (Msb,) and ruHiY~N and riHiY~N , (Msb, K, TA,) with damm and with kesr (Msb, TA) to the r (Msb,) [for the last of which raHiY~N is substituted in the CK,] and A^uroHiY~N , (K, TA,) with damm, and with kesr to the H and teshdeed to the Y (TA,) [in the CK A^aroHiY~N ,] and A^aroHiyapN , (Msb, K,) which is extr., (K,) said by AHát to be wrong, and by IAmb to be anomalous, and by Zj to be not allowable, (Msb,) in the T said to be as though it were a pl. pl., (TA,) or it is pl. of raHaA='N [and therefore regular]: (S:) the dim. is ↓ ruHay~apN . (Zj, Msb.) raHaA Alyadi [or raHaY Alyadi ] signifies The hand-mill. (MA.) ― -b2- [Hence, A molar tooth, or grinder: ] i. q. DirosN ; (S, Msb, K;) pl. A^aroHaA='N i. q. A^aDoraAsN : (S:) [or rather] the A^aroHaA=' , also called the TawaAHin , are the twelve teeth, three on each side [ above and below ], next after the DawaAHik [or bicuspids ]. (Zj, in his “ Khalk el-Insán. ”) ― -b3- [And app. A roller with which land is rolled to crush the clods; as being likened to a mill-stone: see 1 in art. xtm , near the end of the paragraph.] ― -b4- Stones: and a great rock, or mass of stone. (TA.) ― -b5- A round piece of ground, rising above what surrounds it, (S, K,) about as large in extent as a mile: (K:) pl. A^aroHaA='N : (K, TA:) or this latter, i. e. the pl., signifies pieces of rugged ground, less than mountains, round, and rising above what surrounds them: (M, TA:) or raHFA mina AlA^aroDi means a round and rugged place [or piece of ground ] among sands: (Sh, TA:) or a large and rugged [ elevation such as is termed ] qaArap or A^akamap , round, rising above what surrounds it, not spreading upon the surface of the earth, nor producing herbs, or leguminous plants, nor trees. (ISh, TA.) ― -b6- A round cloud; [as being likened to a mill-stone;] (A in art. rjH :) or so raHaY saHaAbK . (S.) ― -b7- The kirokirap [or callous protuberance upon the breast ] of a camel; (T, S, K;) so called because of its roundness: (TA:) pl. A^aroHaA='N : (K:) which likewise signifies the callous protuberances upon the knees of the camel. (T, TA.) ― -b8- The foot ( firosin ) of the camel and of the elephant: pl. A^aroHaA='N . (M, K.) ― -b9- A daAy^irap [app. meaning a circling border ] around the nail. (TA.) ― -b10- The breast, or chest: pl., as in the other senses following, A^aroHaA='N . (K.) ― -b11- Spinage, or spinach; (M, K;) because of the roundness of its leaves. (TA.) ― -b12- (tropical:) A collective body of the members of a household. (ISd, K, TA.) ― -b13- (tropical:) An independent tribe: (K, TA:) A^aroHaA='N (which is its pl., K, TA) signifies (tropical:) independent tribes, that are in no need of others. (S, TA.) ― -b14- (assumed tropical:) A large number of camels, crowding, or pressing, together; (S, K, TA;) also called TaH~aAnapN : (S, TA:) or raHaA AlA_ibili means the collective herd of the camels: and in like manner, raHaA Alqawomi the collective body of the people, or party. (ISk, TA.) ― -b15- raHaY Alqawomi signifies [also] (tropical:) The chief of the people, or party. (T, S, M, K, TA.) [It is added in the TA that 'Omar Ibn-El-Khattáb was called raHaY AlHarobi , as though meaning (assumed tropical:) The chief of war; because of his warlike propensities: but it seems from what here follows, as well as from what precedes, that this may be a mistranscription, for raHaY Alqawomi or raHaY AlEarabi .] ― -b16- raHaY AlHarobi signifies (tropical:) The most vehement part [or the thickest ] of the fight; syn. HawomatuhaA : (S, Msb:) in the K it is said that Alr~aHaY signifies Hawomapu AlHarobi , and muEoZamuhu ; as also ↓ AlmaroHaY : but it seems that there is an omission; for AlHrb is [generally] fem., and in the M it is said that raHaY Almawoti signifies muEoZamuhu [app. meaning the main stress, or the thickest, of death in battle]. (TA.) In a saying relating to 'Alee's having made an end of Aljamali ↓ maroHay , this expression is expl. by A 'Obeyd as meaning The place around which revolved the thickest of the fight ( AlmawoDiEu Al~a*iy daArato Ealayohi raHay AlHarobi ) [in the Battle of the Camel ]. (TA.) And daArato Ealayohi raHay Almawoti [which may be rendered (assumed tropical:) The main stress of death beset him round about ] means death befell him. (Msb, TA.)

sourceDefinition: (Lh, S, K) and A_iranodajN (K) and ↓ yaranodajN (Lh, S) Black skin [or leather ], (S, K,) of which boots are made: termed by Ru-beh, in the following hemistich, ↓ A^arodaAj : kaA^an~amaA surowilona fiY AlA^arodaAji [ As though they were clad in trousers of Arndj ]: (K:) accord. to A' Obeyd, originally Pers., (S,) arabicized, (K,) from ranodaho : (S, K:) one should not say ranodajN : (ISk, S:) accord. to Lh, i. q. daAri$N : or, he adds, as some say, a skin [or leather ] different from that termed dAr$ : or i. q. zaAjN , with which one blackens. (K.) ― -b3- Az mentions Arndj and ↓ yrndj as quadriliteral-radical words. (TA.)

definition: aor. yarodaY , inf. n. radFY , He (a man, TA) perished. (S, M, Msb, K.) [See an ex. in the Kur xx. 17.] ― -b2- And radiYa (AZ, T, M, and so in a copy of the S,) aor. yarodaY , (AZ, T,) inf. n. radFY...
sourceDefinition: aor. yarodaY , inf. n. radFY , He (a man, TA) perished. (S, M, Msb, K.) [See an ex. in the Kur xx. 17.] ― -b2- And radiYa (AZ, T, M, and so in a copy of the S,) aor. yarodaY , (AZ, T,) inf. n. radFY ; (M;) or radaY ; (K, and so in copies of the S;) or both of these verbs; aor. of the latter yarodiY ; (TA;) and ↓ trd~Y ; (S, M, K;) He fell into a well: (AZ, * T, * S, K:) or he tumbled down into a deep hollow, or cavity, or pit: (M:) or ↓ the last of these verbs has this meaning: (Lth, T:) or it signifies he fell into a deep hollow, or cavity, or pit: (Msb:) or he tumbled down (S) from a mountain; (AZ, T, S;) and so the first, or second: (S:) and ↓ trd~Y signifies he fell from a mountain and died. (TA.) A_i*aA ↓ tarad~aY , in the Kur [xcii. 11], means When he falls into the abyss of the fire [ of Hell ]: (T, * TA:) or into the cavity of the grave: or into the lowest depth of Hell: or when he perishes: (Bd:) or when he dies. (T.) ― -b3- And radaY He (a man) went away. (K.) You say, maA A^adoriY A^ayona radaY I know not whither he went away, or has gone away. (S.) -A2- radaAhu , (S, M, K,) aor. yarodiY , (M,) inf. n. radoYN , (TK,) He broke it; (M, K;) namely, a thing with a stone: (M:) or he beat it, [or battered it, ] namely, a stone with a piece of rock, or with a pickaxe, in order to break it. (S.) ― -b2- And He dashed himself against him, or knocked against him, (S, K, TA,) like as the pickaxe knocks against the stone. (TA.) ― -b3- And radaAhu biHajarK , (T, K,) or biHijaArapK , (S,) aor. yarodiY , inf. n. radoYN ; (T;) and radaAhu biHajarK , (K and TA in art. rdw ,) aor. yaroduw , inf. n. radowN , (TA,) with w for the final radical; (K, TA;) [like radaA^ahu , and daraA^ahu ;] He threw at him, or threw at him and hit him, with a stone, or stones. (T, S, M.) [It is also said in the T, with reference to mirodaApN , as signifying a large stone with which other stones are beaten, or battered, Alr~adoYu A_in~amaA huwa rafoEN bihaA waramoYN bihaA ; but I think that rafoEN is a mistranscription for dafoEN ; and that the meaning intended to be expressed by these words is, that radoYN signifies The thrusting with a mirodaAp ; and the throwing it, or with it.] ― -b4- [Hence, app.,] radaY said of a horse, (As, ISk, T, S, M, K,) aor. yarodiY , (As, ISk, T, S, K,) inf. n. radoYN and radayaAnN ; (ISk, S, M, K;) and radaA , (K and TA in art. rdw , [in the CK, w is omitted before the word lugapN in that art.,]) aor. yaroduw ; (TA;) [and, accord. to Freytag, ↓ ArtdY is used in the same sense by Jereer;] He beat, or battered, the ground, ( rajama AlA^aroDa , As, ISk, T, S, ISk, T, S, M, K,) with his hoofs, (M, K, TA,) in running, (As, T,) or in going along, and in running, (M,) or in going a pace between running and vehement walking: (ISk, S:) or radayaAnN signifies the same as taqoriybN : (AZ, T, M: [see 2 in art. qrb :]) or it is [ a manner of going ] between running and walking: (K:) or the running (T, S, M) of the horse (T) or of the ass (S, M) between his A=riY~ [or place of confinement, or the loop to which he is tied, ] and his mutamaE~ak [or place of rolling upon the ground ]; (T, S, M;) thus explained by El-Munteji' Ibn-Nebhán, (T, S,) to As. (S.) In the K, rajamato is erroneously put for rajama ; being app. taken from the M, in which it refers to horses; [not to a single horse;] as does also the pronoun in biHawaAfirihaA , in the same portion of the passage in the K and in the M. (TA.) Accord. to AZ, this is from radayaAnu AljawaAriY , explained in what follows. (Ham p. 221.) ― -b5- You say, radati AljaAriyapu The girl raised one leg and went along upon the other, in play; (K, TA;) and so ↓ Airotadat : (TA:) and AljawaAriY yurodiyna , inf. n. radayaAnN ; (M;) or ↓ yarotadiyna ; (T;) the girls played, (T, M,) raising one leg, (M,) or one of them raising one leg, (T,) and going along upon the other: (T, M:) or radayaAnu AljawaAriY signifies the girls' playing in which one of them raises one leg and steps with the other two steps, and then puts it down and raises the other, doing thus several times. (AZ, Ham p. 221.) And radaY AlgulaAmu The boy raised one leg and leaped, or jumped, [or hopped, ] with the other. (S.) And radaY AlguraAbu , (M, K,) aor. yarodiY , (T,) The crow, or raven, raised one leg and hopped on the other; or leaped along. (T, M, K.) -A3- radato ganamiY My sheep, or goats, increased, or exceeded; as also ↓ A^arodato . (Fr, M, K.) ― -b2- And radayotu EalaY Al$~aYo'i and ↓ Ardyt I exceeded the thing. (M.) And EalaY gayorihi ↓ ArdY It exceeded another thing; as also ArdA^ [q. v.] (M in art. rdA^ .) And radayotu EalaY Alxamosiyna , (S, M, *) and Alv~amaAniyna , (M,) and ↓ Ardyt , (S,) I exceeded [ the age of fifty, and eighty ]. (S, M. *)

definition: A certain garment;
sourceDefinition: A certain garment; (S, Msb;) a kind of miloHafap [or outer wrapping garment ], (M, K,) well known; (K;) one of the garments that are not cut and sewed; (Mgh in art. qTE , and MF voce A_izaArN ;) [ being of a single piece; ] covering the upper half of the body; or lying upon the shoulders and back; (MF voce A_izaArN ;) or falling upon the belly and there ending: (TA voce SiforN :) [a rdA' worn by Mohammad, “thrown over the left shoulder and wrapped round the body under the right arm,” is described as “four cubits long and two cubits and a span wide:” (Sprenger's Life of Mohammad, Part I, English ed., pp. 86 and 87:)] it is of the masc. gender, and it is not allowable to make it fem.: (IAmb, Msb:) the dual is ridaAA=ni and ridaAwaAni the latter being allowable, (S, Msb,) but the former being preferable: (S:) and the pl. is A^arodiyapN : (S, M, Msb:) the ridaA=' is also called ↓ ridaA='apN , (M, K, TA, [in the CK ridAp ,]) like as the A_izaAr is also called A_izaArapq ; (M;) and ↓ mirodaApN , (K, TA, in the CK marodAp ,) of which the pl. is ↓ maraAdK , (TA,) occurring in the saying, maraAdiYa AlHariyri ↓ laA yarotadiY walaA yuraY bisud~api AlA^amiyri A_il~aA liHalobi Al$~aAopi waAlbaEiyri [ He will not wear outer wrapping garments of silk, nor will he be seen at the porch of the commander, or prince, unless for the purpose of milking the sheep, or goat, and the camel ]; (M, TA;) AlmaraAdiY meaning AlA^arodiyap ; (M;) but accord. to Th, it has no sing.: (M, TA:) [or] ↓ maraAdK signifies waist-wrappers; syn. A^uzurN . (K.) ― -b2- Hence, Siforu ridaAy^ihaA , in a description of Umm-Zara, in a trad., meaning (assumed tropical:) Lank in her belly; as though her rdA=' were empty. (TA in art. Sfr .) ― -b3- And gamoru Alr~idaA='i (tropical:) Abounding in beneficence. (T, M, K, TA.) And Eayo$N gamoru Alr~idaA='i (tropical:) A life ample, or plentiful, in its means. (TA.) ― -b4- And ridaA='u Al$~abaAbi (assumed tropical:) The beauty, and softness, tenderness, or delicateness, of youth. (T.) ― -b5- And ridaA='u Al$~amosi (assumed tropical:) The light, (M,) or beauty and light, (T,) of the sun. (T, M.) ― -b6- ridaA='N also signifies (assumed tropical:) A sword; (T, M, K;) [ISd says,] I think, as being likened to the garment thus called; (M;) [i. e.] because it is hung, by its suspensory cords, upon the neck and shoulder [like that garment]. (T.) [See also mirodFY , near the end of the paragraph.] Mutemmem says, laqado kaf~ana AlminohaAlu taHota ridaAy^ihi fatFY gayora miboTaAni AlEa$iy~aAti A^arowaEaA [ Verily El-Minhál has shrouded beneath his sword a young man not voracious in the evenings, when the chief meal is eaten, one who excited the admiration of the beholder ]: for El-Minhál had slain his [the poet's] brother Málik; and when a man slew another who was a celebrated man, he used to lay his sword upon him, in order that his slayer might be known. (M. [But see, in relation to this verse, a long story in the Ham pp. 370-372.]) And El-Khansà says, jaEalota ridaA='aka fiyhaA ximaAraA wadaAhiyapK jar~ahaA jaArimN [ And in many a calamity which a committer of a crime has brought to pass, thou hast made thy sword to be as a covering to the head ]; meaning, thou hast smitten, therein, the necks of thine enemies with thy sword like the xmAr [which means a woman's “muffler” and a man's “turban”]. (T.) ― -b7- Also (assumed tropical:) A bow; (AAF, M, IAth;) because it is borne upon the shoulder, which is the place of the rdA' [properly thus called]. (IAth, TA.) ― -b8- And [for the like reason] (assumed tropical:) The [ ornament called ] wi$aAH [q. v., worn by women]. (T, K.) So in a verse of El-Aashà, cited voce raqoraqa . (T.) ― -b9- And (assumed tropical:) A bier; because it is borne upon the place of the rdA' [properly thus called, i. e., upon the shoulder]. (Ham p. 471.) ― -b10- And (assumed tropical:) Debt; (T, M, K;) because it is [regarded as] a thing that cleaves to the neck of the debtor, like as the rdA' [properly thus called] cleaves to the shoulders of the wearer. (T.) You say, huwa xafiyfu Alr~idaA='i , meaning (tropical:) He is little burdened in respect of debt: and also, in respect of household. (K, * TA.) [See also an ex. voce nasaA='N .] ― -b11- Also (assumed tropical:) Intelligence: ― -b12- and (assumed tropical:) ignorance: (M, K:) both on the authority of IAar: (M:) ― -b13- he says also that it means (assumed tropical:) anything that is the pride, or ornament, of a person; (T, M;) even, (M,) for instance, one's house, and one's father; (T, M;) or one's house and one's beast; (so in the TA;) each of these, he says, is one's rdA' [or (assumed tropical:) pride ]: (T:) thus, (M,) it is (assumed tropical:) a thing that graces: and (assumed tropical:) a thing that disgraces: (M, K:) so that it has two contr. meanings: thus in the K, referring to the meanings of “intelligence” and “ignorance:” but this requires consideration. (TA.)

definition: A stone that is thrown;
sourceDefinition: A stone that is thrown; (S, K;) as also ↓ mirodaApN : (T, S:) or a piece of rock with which date-stones are broken: (Ham p. 417:) and accord. to ISk, ↓ the latter signifies a piece of rock with which stones are broken, (S,) or with which one breaks [ anything ]: (M:) or a stone which the strong man can hardly, or not at all, lift with his hands; [like mirodaA^apN ; (TA in art. rdA^ ;)] with which stones are broken; and with which they beat and soften a rugged place that they hollow out; and with which the hole of the [ lizard called ] Dab~ is broken, or battered, when it is among large stones ( fY qlEp [i. e. fiY qalaEapK ]), which qlEp it softens and demolishes: (En-Nadr, T:) the same word ( mrdAp ) also signifies the stone, (T,) or the piece of rock, (M,) by means of which the Dab~ is guided to its hole: (T, M:) [and accord. to Golius, on the authority of Meyd and the Mirkát el-Loghah, the upper mill-stone: ] the pl. of mirodaApN is ↓ maraAdK : (T:) and this pl. is [also] syn. with maraAmK [app. as pl. of miromaApN , and meaning the arrows thus called; or any missiles ]. (M.) Hence the prov., ↓ Einoda juHori kul~i Dab~K mirodaAtuhu [ Near by the hole of every dabb is its stone that is to be thrown at it, or its stone by means of which it guides itself to that hole ]; applied to a thing that is near at hand, having no obstacle in the way to it; for the dabb will not be guided to its hole, when it goes forth from it and returns to it, except by means of a stone which it places as a mark to point out its hole: (T:) or kul~u ↓ Dab~K Einodahu mirodaAtuhu (S, M, Meyd) i. e. Every dabb has near by it its stone that is to be thrown at it; (S, * Meyd;) for the dabb has little knowledge, therefore it prepares not its hole save by a stone that may be a mark thereof, so that he who seeks it finds the stone that is to be thrown at the dabb near to it; therefore the prov. means that thou shouldst not feel secure from accidents, because calamities are prepared with every time, or period; and it is applied to him who exposes himself to destruction. (Meyd.) Hence also, i. e. from mirodFY in the first of the senses assigned to it above, (S,) or in the second of those senses, (Ham p. 417,) said of a courageous man, A_in~ahu lamirodaY HuruwbK (assumed tropical:) [ Verily he is like the missile of wars ]; (S;) or fulaAnN mirodaY AlHuruwbi (assumed tropical:) [ Such a one is like the crushing stone of the wars ]; or mirodaY AlxuSuwmi , i. e. (assumed tropical:) he whom they throw against the antagonists and who crushes them: (Ham ubi suprà:) and humo maraAdiY AlHuruwbi : [ maraAdK being pl. of mirodFY , as well as of mirodaApN :] (S:) and fulaAnN mirodaY xuSuwmapK waHarobK (assumed tropical:) Such a one is very patient in the endurance of contention and war. (M.) mirodFY is also used as meaning (assumed tropical:) A horse hard like the stone thus called; thus in a verse of 'Antarah: or it there means a horse that runs swiftly; from Alr~adayaAnu [an inf. n. of radaY , q. v.]: or it is from Alr~adaY [inf. n. of radiYa , and syn. therewith], meaning perdition: or it means, in that verse, [like ridaA='N ,] a sword, [as being an instrument of perdition, ] from Alr~adaY . (Ham p. 207.) ↓ mirodaApN , also, (S,) or naAqapN mirodaApN , (TA,) is used as meaning (assumed tropical:) A she-camel like the stone thus called in hardness. (S, TA.) And ↓ maraAdK [as pl. of mirodFY or of mirodaApN ] means also (assumed tropical:) The legs of camels, (Lth, T, M, K,) and of the elephant (Lth, T, K) or of elephants; as being likened to the stones thus called; (M, TA;) or because of their heaviness, and vehemence of tread. (T, TA.) ― -b2- Also mirodFY , (so in the S,) or ↓ murodiY~N , with damm [to the l ] and with shedd [to the Y ], (K,) A pole with which a ship, or boat, is propelled, (S, K,) being in the hand of the sailor: (S:) pl. [of the former] maraAdK , (S,) or [of the latter] maraAdiY~u : (K:) in the dial. of the vulgar midorY [pronounced by them midoraY , without tenween, or midoraA , for midoraA^N ]; pl., with the art., AlmadaAriY [and vulgarly pronounced madaAriY also without the art.]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. rakoDN , He moved, (S, A, K,) or struck with, (Msb,) his leg, or foot: (S, A, Msb, K:) or he struck and hit therewith, like as one strikes and hits therewith a beast. (IAth.) Hence, (S, A, K,) the phrase in the Kur [xxxviii. 41], (S,) AurokuDo birijolika [ Strike thou the ground with thy foot ]: (S, A, K:) or strike thou, and tread, the ground with thy foot. (Sgh.) You say also, rakaDa Alr~ajulu (tropical:) The man struck the ground with his foot: and rakaDati Alxayolu (tropical:) The horses struck the ground with their hoofs: and jaA='ati Alxayolu rakoDFA (tropical:) [ The horses came striking the ground with their hoofs ]: and rakaDati Aljunodabu Alr~amoDaA='a bikuraAEayohaA (tropical:) [ The locusts termed jndb struck the vehemently-hot ground with their two legs ]: and tarakotuhu yarokuDu birijolihi lilomawoti (tropical:) [ I left him striking the ground with his foot previously to death: see also 8]. (A.) [The above-mentioned phrases marked as tropical are so marked on the authority of the A: but the reason of their being so I do not see.] ― -b2- They also said, sometimes, rakaDa AlT~aAy^iru , meaning (assumed tropical:) The bird moved his wings in flying: (S:) the inf. n., rakoDN , signifying (tropical:) the act of moving the wing: (K, TA:) and AlT~aAy^ru yarokuDu bijanaAHayohi (tropical:) The bird moves his wings, and puts them back against his body: (A, TA:) or the former of these two phrases means (assumed tropical:) the bird was quick, or swift, in his flying. (TA.) ― -b3- rakoDN also signifies The act of impelling; syn. dafoEN : and the urging a horse to run, (A, K, TA,) [ by striking ] with his foot or leg: (TA:) the striking a beast with one's feet or legs, to urge him: (Mgh:) or putting him in motion, whether he go on or not. (As.) You say, rakaDotu Alfarasa birijoliY I urged the horse to run, with my foot or leg. (S, O, Msb. *) And rakaDa Ald~aAb~apa , aor. , inf. n. rakoDN , He struck the sides of the beast with his foot or leg. (TA.) And rakaDa Ald~aAb~apa birijolK , and birijolayoni , He struck the beast to urge it with a foot or leg, and with two feet or legs. (A.) ― -b4- And from frequency of usage of the phrase rakaDotu Alfarasa , originated the saying rakaDa Alfarasu , (AZ, * S, Mgh, Msb,) meaning (tropical:) The horse ran: (S, Mgh: *) which some disallow; but without reason, since it has been transmitted by a good authority: (Msb:) it is disallowed by As: (TA:) [and J says,] the correct phrase is rukiDa Alfarasu : (S:) or you say, rukiDa Alfarasu farakaDa huwa , meaning [ The horse was urged to run, ] (assumed tropical:) and he ran: (K:) and rakoDN signifies (assumed tropical:) the act of running: (K, in another place in this art.:) and (assumed tropical:) the act of fleeing: whence, [in the Kur xxi. 12], A_i*aA humo minohaA yarokuDuwna (K) (assumed tropical:) lo, they fled from it, from punishment: (Zj:) or (assumed tropical:) were routed, and fled from it: (Fr:) or they ran from it: (Mgh:) [for] rakaDa Alr~ajulu signifies (assumed tropical:) The man fled, and (assumed tropical:) ran. (ISh.) [Hence,] rakaDati Aln~ujuwmu fiY Als~amaA='i (tropical:) The stars moved along in the sky. (A, TA.) [And hence,] rakoDN also signifies (assumed tropical:) A man's going along by both his legs together. (TA.) ― -b5- You also say, rakaDahu AlbaEiyru (S, A, Msb) (tropical:) The camel struck him with his kind leg: (S, Msb:) like as you say, ramaHahu Alfarasu : (A, Msb: *) but you should not say, [when a camel is the agent,] ramaHahu . (Yaakoob, S.) And rakaDa AlA^aroDa , and Alv~awoba , (assumed tropical:) He struck the ground, and the garment, or piece of cloth, with his foot or leg. (TA.) And AlmaroA^apu tarokuDu *uyuwlahaA waxaloxaAlahaA birijolayohaA A_i*aA ma$ato (tropical:) [ The woman kicks her skirts and her anklets with her feet when she walks ]. (A, TA.) ― -b6- And rakaDati Alqawosu Als~ahoma (tropical:) The bow propelled the arrow. (A, TA.) ― -b7- And rakaDotu Alqawosa (tropical:) I shot with the bow. (A, TA.) ― -b8- And huwa laA yarokuDu AlmiHojana (assumed tropical:) He does not defend himself: (K:) or (assumed tropical:) he is not angry and vexed at a thing, nor does he defend himself. (IAar, L.) ― -b9- And rakaDa Aln~aAra baAlmirokaDi (tropical:) [ He stirred the fire with the markaD ]. (A.)

And zalaja Als~ahomu , aor. , inf. n. zuluwjN and zaliyjN , The arrow fell upon the ground, and did not go straight to the animal at which it was shot. (TA. sourceDefinition: Small in quantity or number: (K:) a mean, paltry, small, or little, gift: (S, TA:) one hat is imperfect, or incomplete: and anything that is not done superlatively, excellently, consummately, thoroughly, or soundly: (TA:) anything low, base, vile, mean, paltry, inconsiderable, or contemptible. (K. [See also muzal~axN .]) ― -b2- Love ( Hub~ [in the CK, erroneously, Hab~ ]) that is not pure, or not genuine. (K.) ― -b3- Having little taste. (Ham p. 404.) ― -b4- Small in body. (Ham ibid.) ― -b5- And hence, (Ham ibid.,) A man (K) deficient, or defective, (K, Ham,) in manliness, or manly virtue or moral goodness, (Ham,) and weak: (TA:) or defective in make: and deficient in prudence, or discretion, and precaution, or sound judgment, or firmness of mind or of judgment: (TA:) and niggardly. (K.) ― -b6- One who is consociated with a people, not being of them: (S, K, TA:) or, as some say, i. q. daEiY~N [i. e. one whose origin, or lineage, is suspected; or an adopted son; &c.]. (TA.) ― -b7- Also Life striven to be retained ( mudaAfaEN ) with a bare sufficiency of the means of subsistence. (TA.)

definition: (S, K) and ↓ zilaAjN (K) [ A kind of latch, or sliding bolt;
sourceDefinition: (S, K) and ↓ zilaAjN (K) [ A kind of latch, or sliding bolt; like mizolaAqN and mizolaAxN ;] a [ thing like the ] migolaAq , except that it is opened with the hand, whereas the mglAq is not to be opened save with the key: (S, K:) a wooden thing by means of which one closes or makes fast [ a door ]: (Ham p. 764; in explanation of the former word:) so called because of the quickness with which it slips (↓ lisuroEapi A@nozilaAjihi ): but ISh describes the kind of mzlAj used by the people of El-Basrah as having a crooked iron key, which slips into a hole in the door, by means of which the door is locked: pl. mazaAliyju . (TA.) -A2- Also the former word, applied to a woman, Having little flesh in her posteriors, or posteriors and thighs; or having small buttocks, sticking together; syn. rasoHaA='u . (S, K.)

definition: A single act of Alz~inaY [i.
sourceDefinition: A single act of Alz~inaY [i. e. fornication or adultery ]: (Msb, TA:) and ↓ zinFY is [used in the same sense, (though properly an inf. n., not of un.,) as is shown by its being] dualized: they say zinayaAni : (TA:) [but this is post-classical:] thus using the dual of zinFY , the lawyers say, qa*afahu bizinayayoni [ He reproached him with two acts of fornication or adultery ]: (Msb, TA:) but [in this instance, and] in the saying ↓ $ahida EalaY zinaA'ayoni , [which is dual of zinaA='N , properly an inf. n. like zinFY ,] or zinayayoni , [ He testified, or gave decisive information, respecting two acts of fornication or adultery, ] the right word is zanoyatayoni . (Mgh.) One says also, huwa A@bonu zanoyapK , and sometimes ↓ zinoyapK , (K,) but the former is the more chaste, (Az, TA,) meaning ↓ A@bonu zinFY [i. e. He is a son of fornication or adultery ]: (K:) or huwa waladu zanoyapK and ↓ zinoyapK , (Mgh, Msb,) and lizanoyapK [ huwa ] and ↓ lizinoyapK , (Mgh,) with fet-h and with kesr, [meaning as above, or wulida lizanoyapK He is, or was, born of fornication or adultery, ] contr. of waladu ri$odapK and liri$odapK , (Mgh,) or contr. of huwa liri$odapK : (Msb:) or ↓ huwa lizinoyapK and lizanoyapK , [ He is the offspring of fornication or adultery, ] contr. of liri$odapK and lira$odapK : (S:) accord. to Fr, one says, huwa ligay~ipK and lizanoyapK and ligayori ra$odapK , [all meaning the same, and] all with fet-h: accord. to Ks, however, one may say ↓ zinoyap and ri$odap , with kesr, but gay~ap only with fet-h: (TA:) ISk says that znyp and gy~p are both with kesr and fet-h. (Msb.)

definition: , (AA, TA,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (AA, TA,) inf. n. tasobiydN , (K, TA,) He shaved off his hair; (AA, K, TA;) as also ↓ sabadahu , (AA, K,) inf. n. sabodN ; (K, TA;) and ↓ Asbdhu , (AA, TA,) inf. n. A_isobaAdN : (K, TA:) or all signify he shaved off his hair and [ so ] removed it utterly: and sabata $aEarahu and sb~thu and Asbthu also have the former signification accord. to AA: (TA:) [and] tasobiydu Alr~aA^osi signifies the removing utterly the hair of the head [ by shaving ]: (S:) or sb~d $aEarahu signifies he shaved off his hair and then left it until it had grown a little: (A'Obeyd, L:) or he removed utterly his hair, making it to be [ shaven ] close to the skin; (A'Obeyd, M, L;) as also sm~dhu . (A'Obeyd, L.) ― -b2- And He let the whole of his hair grow ample and long: thus it has two contr. significations. (M.) ― -b3- And tasobiydN signifies also The combing, or combing down, or letting down and loosing, and then moistening, and leaving, the hair of the head. (Suleymán Ibn-El-Mugheyreh, L, K. *) ― -b4- And The rendering [one's hair] matted, or compacted, and dusty. (M, L.) ― -b5- And [hence, app., the objective complement being meant to be understood,] The leaving off, or neglecting, the anointing of oneself [or of one's hair ], (A'Obeyd, S, K, TA,) and washing: and some say tasomiydN , which signifies the same. (A'Obeyd, TA.) -A2- tasobiydN is also used [intransitively,] as signifying The appearing of the hair of the head: (K:) or the growing after some days: (M:) or sb~d Al$~aEaru means The hair grew so that its blackness appeared after the shaving. (S, M.) ― -b2- And The coming forth of the down [of a young bird]: (M:) or the appearing of the feathers of a young bird. (K.) You say, sb~d Alfaroxu The young bird began to show its feathers, or to become fledged. (S.) ― -b3- And The growing of fresh shoots upon, or among, the old portions of the [plant called] naSiY~ ; as also ↓ A_isobaAdN : (K:) you say [of that plant], sb~d and ↓ Asbd : (TA:) or sb~d Aln~abaAtu The plant had heads coming forth, before the spreading thereof. (M.)

definition: Hair [ of goats ];
sourceDefinition: Hair [ of goats ]; syn. $aEarN ; (As, S, M;) as also ↓ sab~uwdN : (M:) or a small quantity thereof: (K:) or fur [ of camels ]; syn. wabarN . (M.) sourceDefinition: A certain bird, (S, M, K,) having plumage so soft, or smooth, that when two drops of water drop upon it, (S, M, * K,) upon its back, (S, M,) they run off from it; (S, * M, K, * TA;) or such that when a drop of water drops upon its back, it runs [ off ] (M:) the Arabs liken to it a horse when he sweats: (S:) or a certain bird like the eagle: (TA:) or the male eagle: (M, TA:) or the swallow of the desert ( xuT~aAf bar~iY~ ): (As, TA:) or a bird like the xuT~aAf ; when water falls upon it, it runs off from it quickly: so says Aboo-Nasr; and so Skr in his Expos. of the poetry of Hudheyl, on the authority of As: (TA:) said by As to be a certain black bird: (so in a marg. note in one of my copies of the S:) pl. sibodaAnN . (S, M.) ― -b2- Also A piece of cloth with which the watering-trough (K, TA) such as is termed marokuw~ [q. v.] (TA) is rendered close, or firm, [ in its bottom and sides, ] ( yusad~u , [in the L yusobadu , but I know not any apposite meaning of this verb,]) in order that the water may not become turbid: (K:) it is spread therein; and the camels are made to drink [ the water ] above it. (L.) ― -b3- See also sibodapN . -A2- And see sabadN , last sentence.

definition: , [aor. , inf. n. saHotN ,] He extirpated it, eradicated it, exterminated it, or destroyed it utterly; as also ↓ AsHthu : (S, K, TA:) both signify he, or it, made it to go, go away, pass away, or...
sourceDefinition: , [aor. , inf. n. saHotN ,] He extirpated it, eradicated it, exterminated it, or destroyed it utterly; as also ↓ AsHthu : (S, K, TA:) both signify he, or it, made it to go, go away, pass away, or depart; made away with it, did away with it, made an end of it, or destroyed it; namely, a man's property: and the latter, he destroyed utterly what he (a man) possessed. (TA.) You say, saHata AlxitaAna , inf. n. as above; and ↓ AsHthu ; He performed the circumcision so as to remove the prepuce utterly. (TA.) And saHata $aEarahu He removed his hair utterly in shaving and cutting: (A:) and saHata raA^osahu , inf. n. as above; and ↓ AsHthu ; He shaved his head so as to remove the hair utterly. (Lh, TA.) And saHata Al$~aHoma Eani All~aHomi , (aor. as above, K,) He peeled off the fat from the flesh; (S, A, K;) as also saHafahu . (S.) definition: (S, A, Msb, K) and ↓ suHutN , (S, Msb, K,) the former a contraction of the latter, (Msb,) A thing that is forbidden, prohibited, or unlawful;
sourceDefinition: (S, A, Msb, K) and ↓ suHutN , (S, Msb, K,) the former a contraction of the latter, (Msb,) A thing that is forbidden, prohibited, or unlawful; (S, A, K;) and (so in the A, but in the K “ or ”) what is disapproved, abominable, or foul, of gains, (A, K, TA,) that occasions disgrace (K, TA) and bad repute; as the price of a dog, and of wine, and of a pig; (TA;) any pro- perty that is forbidden, not lawful to be gained (Msb, TA) nor to be eaten; (Msb;) anything forbidden, or unlawful, and of bad repute: sometimes it means what is disapproved; and sometimes, what is unlawful; the context showing in which sense it is used: and it is also applied to signify a bribe that is given to a judge or the like: so called because it cuts off blessing: (TA:) in the Kur v. 46, some read lils~uHoti ; and some, lils~uHuti ; (Bd, TA;) and it has also been read as the inf. n., ↓ lils~aHoti : (Bd:) the pl. is A^asoHaAtN . (K.) ― -b2- Also Little, or small, in quantity or number; paltry, mean, or inconsiderable. (K, * TA.) ― -b4- See also masoHuwtN .

definition: A certain plant of the [ season called ] rabiyE : n.
sourceDefinition: A certain plant of the [ season called ] rabiyE : n. un. with p : (JK:) the latter, of which the former is [said to be] the pl., signifies a certain herb, or leguminous plant, (K, TA,) rising upon a stem, having what resembles in form an ear of wheat, in which are grains like those of the yanobuwt [which is variously explained], and a heart, or kernel, ( lubaAb ,) the grain of which is a remedy for wounds: it is also called SaxaA='apN ; but the more approved pronunciation is with s . (TA in art. Sxw .)

[Hence,] waqad~iro fiY A@ls~arodi , in the Kur xxxiv. 10, means And do thou make a due adaptation of the rings in the fabrication of the coats of mail: (Bd, Jel:) or and do thou properly adapt the nails, or pins, and the holes of the rings, [ in the fabrication, ] not making the former thick and the latter small, nor the reverse: (M, Bd, * L:) or Als~arod means Als~amor [i. e. the nailing, or the making firm, or fast, with nails ], (Zj, M, L,) in this instance. (Zj, L.) -A2- Also (assumed tropical:) Coats of mail; (S, M, L, K;) a gen. n. in this sense: (S, K:) [and a single coat of mail; like zarodN and zaradN :] and (tropical:) any other Halaq [properly signifying rings, but here meaning mail ]; (S, A, K;) [i. e.] it signifies also the like of coats of mail, made of Halaq : (M, L:) [said to be] so called because the two extremities of each ring are perforated by the nail, or pin; and these rings are [termed] ↓ Almusoradu : (L:) [if so, the word is an inf. n. used in the sense of a pass. part. n.,] see masoruwdN , [and then as a subst.; and, being originally an inf. n., it is used alike as sing. and pl.; or, as Z says,] it is an inf. n. used as a subst.: (A:) or Als~arodu , as some say, means Als~amoru , [as mentioned above,] and ↓ Als~aradu means AlHalaqu [like Alz~aradu ]. (M.) -A3- Also (tropical:) Consecutive, or following one another: so in the phrase nujuwmN sarodN (tropical:) [ Stars that are consecutive: the epithet retaining the masc. sing. form, though applied to a pl. subst., because originally an inf. n.; like EadolN in the phrase rijaAlN EadolN ]. (A.) So too as an epithet applied to three of the sacred months, in the saying, valaAvapN sarodN wawaAHidN farodN [ Three are consecutive and one is separate ]: (A:) thus an Arab of the desert answered when asked if he knew the sacred months: (S, M, Msb:) the srd are Dhu-l-Kaadeh and Dhu-l-Hijjeh and El-Moharram, and the frd is Rejeb. (S, M.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (TA,) inf. n. sak~N , (K, TA,) i. q. sad~ahu [i. e. He closed or closed up, or he stopped or stopped up, or repaired, and made firm or strong, the thing ]. (K, * TA.) [In the place of sad~uAl$~aYo'i , the explanation of the inf. n. accord. to the reading in the TA, we find in the CK $ad~u Al$~aYo'i : and it seems that $ad~ahu is a correct meaning of sak~ahu ; for it is said that] from masokuwkN as signifying ma$oduwdN is the post-classical phrase sak~u AlA^abowaAbi [i. e. The making fast of doors ]. (TA.) [In the present day, sak~a AlbaAba , aor. and inf. n. as above, means He locked, and he bolted, the door. ] ― -b2- And sak~ahu , (TA,) inf. n. as above, (S, K, TA,) He clamped it ( Dab~abahu ) with iron; namely, a door, (S, K, TA,) and wood. (TA.) -A2- Also sak~ahu , aor. as above, (S, TA,) and so the inf. n., (K, TA,) He cut off his ears. (S, K, * TA.) -A3- sak~a bimaA fiY baTonihi , (TA,) inf. n. as above, (K, TA,) He cast forth what was in his belly; (K, * TA;) muted, or dunged; (TA;) said of an ostrich: (K, TA:) and so saj~a . (TA.) And sak~a bisaloHihi , (AA, TA,) inf. n. as above, (K, TA,) He cast forth his excrement, or ordure, (AA, K, TA,) in a thin state; (AA, * K, TA;) as also zak~a , (AA, TA,) and hak~a . (TA.) And huwa yasuk~u , inf. n. as above, He voids thin excrement or ordure; (As, S, TA;) as also yasuj~u , inf. n. saj~N . (As, TA.) And A^axa*ahu sak~u [ He was taken with a looseness of the bowels; ] he had thin evacuations of the bowels; expl. by qaEada maqaAEida riqaAqFA : and A^axa*ahu sak~N fiY baTonihi [signifies the same; or] his bowels became loose; as also saj~N ; so says Yaakoob; and he asserts it to be formed by substitution; but which of the two is so formed is unknown. (TA.) ― -b2- sak~a fiY AlA^aroDi He went at random in the land, or country, not knowing whither to go, and was perplexed. (Ibn-'Abbád, O. [See also 7.]) ― -b3- One says also, A^ayona tasuk~u Whither goest thou? (Ibn-'Abbád, O.) ― -b4- maA sak~a samoEiY mivolu *`lika AlkalaAmi The like of that speech has not entered my ear, or ears: and fiY masaAmiEiY mivoluhu ↓ maAA@sotak~a The like of it has not entered my ears. (TA.) -A4- sak~a , [sec. pers., app., sakukota ,] aor. , (TA,) inf. n. suk~N , (K, TA,) It (one's nature, or disposition,) was, or became, base, ignoble, mean, or sordid. (K, * TA.) -A5- sak~a , (Msb, TA,) sec. pers. sakikota , (Msb, K, TA, [in the CK, erroneously, sakikota ,]) inf. n. sakakN , (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA,) said of a man, &c., (K,) (assumed tropical:) He was small in the ear, (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA,) with a sticking thereof to the head, and small projection thereof: (K, TA:) or he was short in the ear, with a sticking thereof to the part behind it: (TA:) or he was small in the quwf [here meaning either the upper part or the helix (in the CK quwb )] of the ear, and narrow in the ear-hole. (K, TA.) And (assumed tropical:) He was, or became, deaf. (K, TA.)

definition: A well narrow (Lth, AZ, As, S, O, K) in its cavity, or interior, (Lth, O,) or from its top to its bottom, (AZ, S, O,) or in its aperture;
sourceDefinition: A well narrow (Lth, AZ, As, S, O, K) in its cavity, or interior, (Lth, O,) or from its top to its bottom, (AZ, S, O,) or in its aperture; as also ↓ sak~N , and ↓ sakuwkN : (K:) or a well even in its cavity, or interior, and in its casing: or, accord. to Fr, one well, or strongly, or compactly, cased, and narrow; the pl. of suk~N is sikaAkN ; and the pl. of ↓ sakuwkN is suk~N , so that the latter is both a sing. and a pl. (TA.) ― -b2- And A narrow road: (I'Abbád, O:) or a road stopped up: (K:) or a road narrow and stopped up. (Lh, TA.) ― -b3- See also sak~N . ― -b4- Also The hole of the scorpion, (Ibn- 'Abbád, S, O, K,) in the dial. of the BenooAsad; (Ibn-'Abbád, O;) and of the spider, (O, K,) likewise, because of its narrowness. sourceDefinition: A ploughshare; i. e. the iron thing with which the ground is ploughed; (S, TA;) the iron appertenance of the plough. (K.) Hence the trad., maA daxalati Als~ik~apu daAra qawomi A_il~aA *al~uwA [ The ploughshare enters not the abode of a people, or party, but they become abased ]; meaning, in consequence of the violence and the demands that the agriculturists experience from the ruling power. (TA.) ― -b2- And A die, i. e. an engraved piece of iron, (S, * Msb, K, TA,) having an inscription upon it, (TA,) with which dirhems and deenárs are stamped, (S, * Msb,) or upon which pieces of money ( daraAhim ) are struck: (K:) pl. sikakN . (Msb.) ― -b3- And, because stamped therewith, A coined dirhem, and deenár; (TA;) which latter is called [also] ↓ sikiY~N , (O, K, TA,) [in the CK sakiY~ , but it is] with kesr. (TA.) -A2- Also A row ( TariyqapN muSoTaf~apN , S, O, Msb, or saTorN , K, or saTorN maSoTaf~N , TA) of palm-trees. (S, O, Msb, K, TA.) Hence their saying, (S,) or the saying of the Prophet, (O,) xayoru AlmaAli muhorapN maA^omuwrapN A^awo sik~apN maA^obuwrapN , (S, in the O sk~p mA^bwrp Aw mhrp mA^mwrp ,) meaning [ The best of property is ] a prolific filly (TA) or a row of palm-trees fecundated: (S, TA:) or, accord. to As, sk~p mA^bwrp here signifies a ploughshare properly prepared [ for ploughing ]; and, he says, the meaning is, that the best of property is a brood [of a mare] or seed-produce. (S.) [It has been suggested to me that, if Tryqp in the explanation above have the signification here assigned to it, the epithet mSTf~p is redundant; and therefore that Tryqp alone may be the proper explanation, and may mean in this case, as it does in many others, a tall palm-tree, or the tallest of palm-trees, or a smooth palm-tree, or a palm-tree the head of which is reached by the hand; and that mSTf~p may have been added in consequence of misunderstanding, and sTr substituted for Tryqp for the same reason: but I think it much more probable that the epithet has been added because Tryqp is ambiguous; and this is confirmed by what here follows.] ― -b2- Also A zuqaAq [meaning street ]: (S, O, * Msb:) or [rather] a wide zuqaAq : (Msb:) or an even road, (K, TA,) [or street, ] of such as are termed A^aziq~ap [pl. of zuqaAq ]: (TA:) so called because the houses therein form a row or rows [on either side]; (O, TA;) being likened to a sik~ap of palm-trees: (TA:) [in the present day, often applied to a highway, and to any road: ] pl. sikakN [as above]: (O:) and ↓ sakaAy^iku is syn. with [ sikakN as meaning] A^aziq~apN . (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also, app., one says,] AijoEali AlA^amora sik~apF waAHidapF (assumed tropical:) Make thou the affair, or case, [ uniform, or] one uniform thing. (Fr, TA in art. bA^j .) ― -b4- And A^axa*a AlA^amora bisik~atihi , (K,) and A^adorakahu bisik~atihi , (TA,) (assumed tropical:) [ He took the thing, and he attained it, in its proper way, or] when it was possible. (K, TA.) ― -b5- And fulaAnN SaEobu Alsik~api (tropical:) Such a one will not remain quiet, or still, or steady, by reason of hastiness of temper. (Ibn- 'Abbád, Z, O, TA.) -A3- Also The house [or station ] of the bariyd [or messenger that journeys on a beast of the post, or messengers on beasts of the post: it is likewise called sik~apu Albariydi : see bariydN ]: and A^aSoHaAbu Als~ikaki , occurring in a letter of 'Omar Ibn-'Abd-El-'Azeez, means the burud [or messengers on beasts of the post ] who are stationed there to be sent on affairs of importance. (Mgh.) sik~apu Albariydi is well known [as having the meaning assigned to it above: and also as meaning The space, or distance, between each station of the messengers above mentioned and the station next to it: see, again, bariydN ]. (Ibn-'Abbád, O.)

sourceDefinition: Small in the ear, (Mgh, K,) with a sticking thereof to the head, and small projection thereof: (K:) or short in the ear, with a sticking thereof to the part behind it: (TA:) or small in the qwf [meaning either the upper part or the helix ] of the ear, and narrow in the ear-hole: (K:) applied to a man, (Mgh, K,) &c.: (K:) fem. sak~aA='u : (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K:) applied [to a woman, as is implied in the K, and to a female bird, and particularly to a female ostrich, and] to a single bird of the species called qaTFA , because having no ear [apparent or projecting], (TA,) and to a she-goat, meaning, with the lawyers, having no ear except the ear-hole, or, accord. to El-Kudooree, naturally earless: (Mgh:) and applied to an ear, as meaning small: (S, Msb:) pl. suk~N : applied [to human beings, &c., more commonly to birds, and particularly] to ostriches, (K,) and to birds of the species called qaTFA : (TA:) it is said that every sak~aA=' is oviparous, and every $arofaA=' is viviparous; the former meaning a female that has no ear (S, O) apparent, or external; (O;) and the latter, “a female that has an ear (S, O) apparent, or external, (O,) though it be slit.” (S.) A rájiz says, layolapu Hak~ Klayosa fiyhiA $ak~u A^aHuk~u Hat~aY saAEidiY munofak~u A^asoharaniY AlA^usayowidu AlA^asak~u [ A night of scratching: there is no doubt respecting it: I scratch so that my fore arm, or my upper arm, (for sAEd is used in both of these senses,) is dislocated: the little black thing without ears having rendered me sleepless ]: he means the fleas, using the sing. as a gen. n. (TA.) ― -b2- Also Having the ears cut off. (TA.) [This seems to be the primary, though not a usual, signification.] ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) [ Having the ears stopped up: (see 8:) or] deaf. (K.) It is applied in this sense to the ostrich, because [they say that] he does not hear. (Lth, TA.) ― -b4- And AlA^asak~u was the name of A certain horse. (O, K.) ― -b5- See also sak~N .

sourceDefinition: or salFA [thus differently written, the former the more correct, unless the word be derived from Als~alowapu , as it is said to be in the Ham p. 656, but this is improbable,] The secundine; i. e. the skin, [or membrane, ] (M, K,) or thin skin, (S,) in which is the fœtus, or young, [ in the womb, ] (S, M, Msb, K,) of human beings, and of horses and camels, (M,) or of human beings and of cattle, (K,) or [peculiarly] of cattle, (T, S,) that of human beings being termed ma$iymapN : (TA:) it is pulled off from the face of the young camel at the time of the birth, or else it kills it, like as it does when it becomes disrupted in the belly: when it comes forth, the she-camel is safe, and so is the young one; but if it becomes disrupted in the belly, she perishes, and so does the young one: (S:) pl. A^asolaA='N . (M, Msb, K.) [Hence,] one says, AinoqaTaEa Als~alaY fiY AlbaToni (assumed tropical:) [ The secundine became disrupted in the belly ]; (S, Meyd, K;) i. e. artifice departed [or came to an end]; (S;) a prov. applied in the case of an affair's becoming beyond one's power of accomplishment, and coming to an end; (Meyd;) like the saying, balaga Als~ik~iynu AlEaZoma [The knife reached to the bone]. (S, K.) And huwa A=kilu AlA^asolaA='i (assumed tropical:) [ He is the eater of secundines ]; meaning he is low, base, vile, or sordid. (TA.) (S, Meyd.)

definition: An arrow; i. e. one of what are called nabol , (Msb, K, TA,) having the iron head [ and the feathers ] affixed: (TA:) the sahom before it has its feathers and its iron head affixed to it is...
sourceDefinition: An arrow; i. e. one of what are called nabol , (Msb, K, TA,) having the iron head [ and the feathers ] affixed: (TA:) the sahom before it has its feathers and its iron head affixed to it is [generally] called qidoHN : (S and K in art. qdH :) accord. to some it signifies the iron head itself; i. q. naSolN ; (Msb;) ISh says that this is its meaning; and he says, if one pick up a nSl , you say “ What is this sahom with thee? ” but if one pick up a qidoH , you do not say thus; and the naSol is the broad and long sahom , and may be nearly of the length of the space between the extremity of the thumb and that of the fore finger when they are stretched out; and the mi$oqaS is of half the size of the naSol : (TA:) [but this meaning of sahomN seems to be very rare, and little known:] the pl. [of mult.] is sihaAmN (S, TA) and [of pauc.] A^asohumN . (TA.) [Hence,] sahomu Alr~aAmiY (assumed tropical:) [ The arrow of the archer ], (K,) or [simply] Als~ahomu [ the arrow ], (Kzw,) a certain constellation, (K, * Kzw,) [namely Sagitta, ] one of the northern constellations, composed of five stars, between the bill [meaning the star β ] of Ald~ajaAjapu [which is Cygnus ] and Aln~asoru AlT~aAy^ru [which consists of the stars α and β and γ of Aquila ], in the Great Milky Way, having its head towards the east and its notch towards the west; and its length, as it appears to the eye, when it is in the middle of the sky, is about two cubits ( naHowu *iraAEayoni : see *iraAEN ). (Kzw.) ― -b2- Also The qidoH [or featherless and headless arrow ] with which one casts, or draws, lots, (IAth, Mgh, TA,) in the game called Almayosir ; (IAth, Mgh, TA;) and the qidoH with which one plays at a game of hazard [ of any kind; i. e. an arrow for sortilege, and a gaming-arrow ]; the primary meaning of the word being the missile sahom ; (Mgh;) or the primary meaning is the qidoH with which one casts, or draws, lost in the game called Almayosir : (IAth, TA:) pl. sihaAmN (K) [and A^asohumN , as above]. See a verse cited voce raqiybN . ― -b3- Then applied to The thing won by him whose arrow is successful [ in the game above mentioned ]. (IAth, TA.) ― -b4- And then (IAth, TA) applied also to A lot, share, or portion, (S, IAth, Mgh, Msb, K, TA,) whatever it be; (IAth, TA;) as also ↓ suhomapN : (S, Msb, K:) pl. of the former suhomaAnN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and sihaAmN [both pls. of mult.] and A^asohumN [pl. of pauc.] (Mgh, Msb, TA) and [quasi-pl. n.] ↓ suhomapN , (M, K, TA,) this last like A^uxowapN . (TA.) It is said in a trad., kaAna lahu sahomN mina Alganiymapi $ahida A^awo gaAba [ There was, or is, for him a share of the spoil whether he were, or be, present or absent ]. (TA.) And one says, fulaAnK mino h`*aA ka*aA ↓ suhomapu The share of such a one, of this, is such a thing: and it may be from Als~ihaAmu meaning the arrows ( qidaAH ) that are shuffled among the persons competing in sortilege, in order that each one may appropriate to himself what comes forth for him as his share. (Ham p. 579.) ― -b5- sahomu Als~afiynapi [ The mast of the ship: so called as being likened to an arrow, because the curved yard of the sail, resembling a bow, is suspended from the top]: (S, and K in art. dql :) [in like manner] called in Pers. tiyri ki$otiY . (PS in that art.) ― -b6- sahomu Albayoti The beam ( jaAy^iz ) of the house or chamber; (S, K;) [similarly] called in Pers. tiyr . (S voce jaAy^izN , q. v.) ― -b7- sahomN also signifies The measure of six cubits [as used] in men's sales and purchases in their measurings of land. (K.) ― -b8- And A stone which is placed upon the entrance of a chamber constructed for the purpose of capturing therein the lion, so that, when he enters it, it falls upon the the entrance and closes it. (K, * TA.) [The word in this sense is also mentioned in the K as written with $ .]

definition: A shower, or fall, or what pours forth at once or without intermission, of rain (S, A, O, K) &c.
sourceDefinition: A shower, or fall, or what pours forth at once or without intermission, of rain (S, A, O, K) &c.: (S, O:) or of rain with hail; for otherwise this term is not applied to rain: (ISd, TA:) pl. $aA=biybu : (S, A, O, K: *) this is the pl. of $uw^obuwbN (K, TA) in all its senses: (TA:) or rain that falls upon one place and misses another; like najowN and najaA='N . (AZ, TA.) ― -b2- [ A thin, not wide, cloud, of which the rain falls with vehemence. (Freytag, from the Deewán of the Hudhalees.)] ― -b3- A heat, or an unintermitted act, of running. (TA.) ― -b4- Sharpness, vehemence, force, or strength, of anything: (K:) violence, or vehemence, of impetus or pushing or driving, (S, A, O, K,) of rain, (A,) or of anything. (K.) Kaab Ibn-Zuheyr says, speaking of a he-ass and she-asses, A_i*aA maA A@notaHaAhun~a $uw^obuwbuhu raA^ayota lijaAEiratayohi guDuwnaA i. e. When he runs vehemently [ towards them, or rather when his vehemence of running is directed towards them ], thou seest a wrinkling [or wrinkles ] in his jaAEirataAni [dual of jaAEirapN , q. v.]. (S, O.) ― -b5- The first appearance [or bloom ] of beauty. (K.) One says of a girl, or young woman, A_in~ahaA laHasanahu $aA=biybi Alwajohi Verily she is goodly in respect of the first appearances [or bloomings ] of beauty of countenance in the eye of the beholder. (O.) ― -b6- The vehemence of the heat of the sun. (K.) ― -b7- And The Tariyqap of the sun: (K:) $aA=biybu Al$~amosi signifies the lines, or streaks, ( TaraAy^iq ,) of the sun when it rises. (O.) ― -b8- $aA=biybu AlS~amogi What flows, of the [ manna, or gum, called ] migofar [q. v.], and remains like strings, or threads, between the trees and the ground. (T, L.) [See also maEaAbiybu .]

sourceDefinition: [ More, and most, unlucky, inauspicious, unfortunate, or unprosperous ]. The Arabs say, A^a$oA^amu kul~i A@moriy^ K bayona laHoyayohi , (Meyd, TA,) as some relate it, or, as others relate it, fak~ayohi , which means the same, (Meyd,) [app. meaning accord. to the TA, The most unlucky thing of every man is between his two jaws, or the two lateral portions of his lower jaw; but it is said that] A^a$oA^amu is here used in the sense of $uw^omN [i. e. the unluckiness, &c.]; and in a similar manner [the contr.] A^ayomanu is used [in the sense of yumon ]: so says AHeyth: (Meyd:) the prov. meaning the tongue. (AHeyth, TA.) The fem. is $uw^omaY . (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (TA,) Alyadu Al$~uw^omaY The left hand or arm; contr. of AlyumonaY ; (K, TA;) i. q. Al$~imaAlu . (TA.) It is said in a trad., respecting camels, laA yaA^otiY xayoruhaA A_il~aA mino jaAnibihaA AlA^a$oA^ami [ Their goodness comes not save from their left side ]: i. e. they are milked and mounted only from the left side. (TA.) ― -b3- See also ma$ow^uwmN , in three places. ― -b4- Zuheyr, in the following saying, fatunotajo lakumo gilomaAna A^a$oA^ama kul~uhumo kaA^aHomari EaAd K vum~a turoDiEo fatafoTimo uses it in the sense of the inf. n. $uw^om ; (S;) meaning gilomaAna $uw^omK : (S, and EM p. 124:) he says, And it, i. e. war, will bring forth for you boys of ill luck, or evil omen; all of them like Ahmar of' Ád: then it will suckle these boys, and wean them: by Ahmar of ' Ád, he means Ahmar of Thamood, for Ahmar was the surname of him who hamstrung the she-camel of Sálih, and his name was Kudár: he says thus for the sake of the measure: or, as some say, Thamood were called 'Ád-el-Ákhireh. (EM.)

definition: Certain trees, (K,) a species of the trees of the mountains, (S,) meaning of the mountains of the saraAp , [the mountain-range extending from near 'Arafát to Nejrán in El-Yemen,] for there they grow,...
sourceDefinition: Certain trees, (K,) a species of the trees of the mountains, (S,) meaning of the mountains of the saraAp , [the mountain-range extending from near 'Arafát to Nejrán in El-Yemen,] for there they grow, (TA,) of which bows are made: (S, K:) AHn says, One acquainted with [the kind of trees called] the $wHT has informed me that it grows in the manner of the A^aroz [or pine-tree ], many rods growing from one stem; its leaves are thin and long, and it has a fruit like the long grape, [the word here rendered “ grape ” is Enbp , but it has been altered in the MS., and may therefore be incorrect,] except that its extremity is more slender, and it is soft, and is eaten: (TA:) or i. q. naboEN : (IB:) or a species of the naboE , (K,) of which bows are made: (TA:) or the $wHT and nbE and $iroyaAn are one; the name varying according to the excellence of their places of growth; what is upon the summit of the mountain being called nbE ; what is upon its base, or foot, or lowest or lower part, $ryAn ; and what is in the depressed tract by its base, $wHT : (Mbr, Az, K:) IB says the same with respect to the nbE , but that the $wHT is that which is upon the lowest part of the mountain; and this is confirmed by what is said by AZ and others: El-Ghanawee El-Aarábee says, the nbE and $wHT and saraA=' are one: as to the $ryAn , no one holds it to be of the nbE except Mbr: Aboo-Ziyád says that bows are made of the $ryAn , and they are good, but of a black colour tinged with redness: and AHn says in one place, that the nbE and $wHT are yellow in the wood, heavy in the hand; and when they become old, they become red: (TA:) the n. un. is with p . (K.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor. , (A, Msb, K,) inf. n. $uxuwSN , (S, Msb, K,) He, or it, rose; or became raised, or elevated. (S, A, Msb, K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] It (a star) rose. (K.) And $axaSa lahu $axoSN [ A figure seen from a distance rose to his view ]. (TA in art. zwl .) ― -b3- $axaSa baSaruhu (S, Mgh, Msb, K, [in some copies of the K, baSarahu , but this occurs afterwards in that work,]) is said when a man opens his eyes and then does not move his eyelids; [and signifies (tropical:) His eyes, or lit., his eye, became fixedly open: ] (S, K: *) or it signifies his eye became raised: (Msb:) or his sight became stretched and raised. (Mgh.) [See the Kur xiv. 43, and xxi. 97.] You say, $axaSa A_ilayoka baSariY (tropical:) [ My eye, or eyes, became fixedly open, or raised, or my sight became stretched and raised, towards thee ]. (A.) And $axaSa baSaru Almay~iti , (A,) inf. n. as above, (IAth,) (tropical:) [ The eye, or eyes, of the dying man became fixedly open: or] the eyelids of the dying man became raised upwards, and he looked intently, and became disquieted, or disturbed. (IAth.) ― -b4- saxaSati Alkalimapu mina Alfami (assumed tropical:) The word, or sentence, rose [ from the mouth ] towards the palate: this is sometimes natural: i. e., one's raising his voice, and not being able to lower it. (K.) ― -b5- $axaSa Als~ahomu (inf. n. as above, Msb,) (tropical:) The arrow rose [ so as to deviate ] from the butt, or object of aim: (K:) or the arrow passed beyond the butt, or object of aim, going above it: (A, Msb:) or rose in the sky. (ISh.) ― -b6- $axaSa (aor. as above, Msb, and so the inf. n., S, Msb,) also signifies He went, or went away, from one town or country to another: (S, A, K:) or he went forth from one place to another, (Msb,) or from his place of alighting or abiding: (TA:) or [so accord. to the TA, but in the K “ and ”] he journeyed upwards. (K, TA.) You say also, $axaSa mino qawomihi He went forth from his people: and $axaSa A_ilayohimo he returned to them. (TA.) ― -b7- Also, (M, K,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (M,) It (a thing) rose; or swelled; or became swollen: (M:) it (a wound) rose, and became swollen: (M, K:) [ it was, or became, protuberant, or prominent. ] -A2- $axaSa baSarahu , (Msb, K, TA,) or $axaSa bibaSarihi , (Mgh,) or both, (TA, [in which it is said to be tropical,]) and $axaSa bibaSarihi A_ilaY Als~amaA='i , (Msb,) or $axaSa [alone], (so in a copy of the A, [in which it is mentioned among proper expressions,]) (assumed tropical:) He raised his eye, or sight, (K, TA,) towards the sky, and did not move his eyelids; said of a dying man: (TA:) or he stretched and raised his sight: (Mgh:) or he opened his eyes, (A, Msb,) and did not move his eyelids, (A,) or [ looking fixedly, ] not moving his eyelids. (Msb.) ― -b2- ya$oxaSu biSawotihi falaA yaqodiru EalaY xafoDihi (assumed tropical:) [ He raises his voice, and is not able to lower it ]. (K.) ― -b3- $uxiSa bihi , (S, K,) coordinate to EuniYa , (K,) or $uxiSa [alone], (so in a copy of the A,) or $axiSa bihi A^amorN , coordinate to taEiba , inf. n. $axaSN , (Msb,) (tropical:) [ He was disquieted by a thing that happened to him: or] a thing that disquieted him happened to him: (S, A, K:) or a thing happened to him and disquieted him: (Msb:) as though he were raised from the ground by reason of his disquietude. (TA.) [See also 4.] -A3- $axuSa , aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. $axaASapN , or this is a simple subst., [for] ISd says, I have not heard a verb of which it may be the inf. n., (TA,) [if used, signifying] He (a man, S) was, or became, big, bulky, or corpulent. (S, K.)
